pedagogy.summary: Factorising by common factors is the inverse of expanding: rewrite a sum as a product by pulling out the highest common factor (HCF) of every term, leaving a bracket that itself has no common factor. 6x+9 = 3(2x+3). It is best taught alongside expanding, using the reverse area model (arrange the terms into a rectangle; the common side is the factor, and the WIDEST rectangle uses the HCF) and always checking by expanding the answer back. The signature errors are taking a common factor that is not the HIGHEST (incomplete factorisation) and dropping or mis-dividing a term.
bestPractices: Teach it as the reverse of expanding — do an expansion, then run it backwards — and always CHECK by expanding the factorised form.
Find the HCF of the coefficients (and any common variable) first; stress 'fully' means no common factor is left inside the bracket.
Use the reverse area/array model: the terms tile a rectangle whose common side is the factor; the HCF gives the neatest single rectangle.
Divide EVERY term by the factor — 6x÷3 and 9÷3 — and write each result inside the bracket; a dropped term is the classic slip.
Extend to a common variable factor, e.g. x²+3x = x(x+3), so 'common factor' includes letters, not just numbers.
keyRepresentations: Reverse area/array model (terms arranged into a rectangle; common side = factor)
HCF via prime factors or factor lists of the coefficients
Side-by-side expand/factorise pair showing the inverse relationship
commonMisconceptions: Takes a common factor that is not the HIGHEST: 12x+8 → 2(6x+4) instead of 4(3x+2) — 'factorised' but not fully.
Drops or fails to divide a term: 6x+9 → 3(2x) or 3(2x+9) (the 9 not divided).
Only spots numeric factors and misses a common variable: x²+3x left unfactorised or written 3(x²)... .
Does not check by expanding, so an incorrect factorisation goes unnoticed.
Confuses factorising (→ product) with simplifying/collecting (→ fewer terms).

learn.summary: Factorising by common factors is the inverse of expanding: rewrite a sum as a product by pulling out the highest common factor (HCF) of every term, leaving a bracket with no remaining common factor, e.g. 6x+9 = 3(2x+3). Teach it alongside expanding, use a reverse area/array model (arrange the terms into a rectangle whose common side is the factor; the HCF gives the single rectangle with the LARGEST common side — the most compact block, not the long thin strip a smaller factor leaves), and always check by expanding the answer back. Signature errors are taking a factor that is not the highest (incomplete factorisation) and dropping or mis-dividing a term. Extend 'common factor' to a shared letter, e.g. x²+3x = x(x+3).

activities.title: Build the rectangle with the largest common side: the reverse area model
feedback: If you pulled out 2 from 12x+8: look inside the bracket — 6x and 4 are both still even, so a factor of 2 can still be shared. Ask 'is there still a number that divides everything in the bracket?' and pull it out too, or find the HCF of 12 and 8 first (it is 4).
If you wrote 3(2x) for 6x+9, a term has gone missing: every original term must appear as factor × bracket-entry. 9 must be divided too — 9÷3 = 3 — giving 3(2x+3).
If you wrote 3(2x+9), the 9 was not divided: divide each term by 3, then expand back to test — 3(2x+3) = 6x+9, but 3(2x+9) = 6x+27.
To check any answer, multiply it out: if it does not give the expression you started with, a term was dropped or mis-divided.
For x²+3x, a number alone is not the common factor — every term also contains an x, so x(x+3) is the fully factorised form.
activities.rationale: Arranging terms into a rectangle is intended to make 'find the HCF' concrete as 'make the rectangle with the largest common side that leaves nothing to share', and pairing it with an expand-back step is intended to build the inverse relationship with expanding and the self-check habit. Area representations are documented as linking the two directions.
sourceClaims: Factorising is best taught explicitly as the inverse of expanding/the distributive law ('factor × factor = product', 3(a+b)=3a+3b; pose the reverse question 'if the product is 3a+3b, what are the factors?'), and the distributive law's 'every term inside the brackets is multiplied by the term outside' principle is what prevents dropping/mis-dividing a term when working the inverse (factorising) direction; the objective is to factorise expressions where there is a common factor (e.g. 3a+12b).
Factorising is the inverse of expanding a single bracket; the correct expansions the expand-back check relies on (e.g. 2(n+3)=2n+6) are documented, and area representations link the two directions.
learnerActions: Take the tiles for 12x + 8 (twelve x-tiles and eight unit tiles) and try to arrange them into one solid rectangle.

First try a common side of 2: notice the result is a long 2-by-(6x+4) strip. Check whether each row could be split again into equal parts — it can, because 6x and 4 both still divide by 2, so the strip can be regrouped into a taller rectangle. That means 2 is a common factor but not the highest, so 2(6x+4) is not fully factorised.
Now try a common side of 4: the tiles form a compact 4-by-(3x+2) block with nothing left to share, giving 12x + 8 = 4(3x + 2).
Divide EVERY original term by the factor you pulled out (12x÷4 = 3x and 8÷4 = 2) and write each result inside the bracket.
Use an 'expand back' action to re-spread the rectangle into 12x + 8 and confirm the product equals what you started with.
Repeat with a shared letter: arrange x² + 3x and find that the common side is x, giving x(x + 3).
activities.intendedInsight: The highest common factor is 'the biggest common side that leaves nothing left to share', so fully factorised means no common factor remains inside the bracket; factorising and expanding are inverse moves.

activities.title: Factorise then expand-back: the routine check
feedback: 2(6x+4) is a correct factorisation but NOT fully factorised: 6x and 4 both still divide by 2, so the HCF (4) was not used. Fully factorised is 4(3x+2).
If expanding back does not return the original, look for a term that was dropped from the bracket or a term that was not divided by the factor.
Finding the HCF first (here 4 for 12x+8, 3 for 6x+9) lets you factorise fully in one step instead of stopping early.
Factorising undoes expanding: expanding turns a product into a sum; factorising turns a sum back into a product.
activities.rationale: Judging 'fully vs not fully' and verifying by expanding back are intended to target the two signature errors (incomplete factorisation and dropped/mis-divided terms). Partial factorisation is a documented student response.
sourceClaims: Partial / not-fully factorisation — removing only one available common factor and stopping (on 9x²+6x, taking out only the 3 or only the x rather than the full 3x) — is a documented, recognised student response, explicitly built into the mark scheme as a one-mark partial factorisation.
Factorising is the inverse of expanding a single bracket; the correct expansions the expand-back check relies on (e.g. 2(n+3)=2n+6) are documented, and area representations link the two directions.
learnerActions: Given 6x + 9, find the HCF of 6 and 9 using prime factors or factor lists, then write 6x+9 = 3(2x+3), dividing each term by 3.
Immediately expand your product back out and confirm it returns the original expression.
Decide whether a given bracket is fully factorised: is 2(6x+4) fully factorised? Explain how you can tell.
Explain in your own words what factorising is 'undoing'.
activities.intendedInsight: A factorisation is only complete when the bracket shares no further common factor, and expanding back is the way to catch dropped or mis-divided terms.

activities.title: Annotated worked example: where each number comes from
feedback: Check that each original term (6x and 9) is accounted for inside the bracket: 6x÷3 = 2x and 9÷3 = 3. If one is missing, the factorisation is wrong, because expanding it back will not give the original expression.
This worked example is fixed and cannot be re-arranged, so follow it up by factorising a fresh expression yourself and expanding it back.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal annotated example is intended to make the origin of each part explicit and to support learners before they search for the HCF independently; it shows the parts but does not let the learner search for the HCF by building, so it works as a scaffold rather than the main task.
sourceClaims: Factorising is best taught explicitly as the inverse of expanding/the distributive law ('factor × factor = product', 3(a+b)=3a+3b; pose the reverse question 'if the product is 3a+3b, what are the factors?'), and the distributive law's 'every term inside the brackets is multiplied by the term outside' principle is what prevents dropping/mis-dividing a term when working the inverse (factorising) direction; the objective is to factorise expressions where there is a common factor (e.g. 3a+12b).
learnerActions: Study the worked line 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3) and reveal, one piece at a time, where the 3, the 2x and the 3 inside the bracket each come from (3 is the HCF; 2x = 6x÷3; 3 = 9÷3).
Trace each original term to its matching entry inside the bracket, confirming no term was dropped.
activities.intendedInsight: Every term in the sum maps to factor × a term in the bracket, which is why no term may be dropped or left undivided.

constraints: 'Fully factorised' means no common factor (number or letter) remains inside the bracket; stopping at a smaller common factor is incomplete.
Every original term must be divided by the factor and appear inside the bracket; a dropped or undivided term is the classic slip.
Always verify by expanding the product back to the original sum before accepting an answer.
The annotated worked example is a fixed scaffold: it displays the parts but cannot let the learner search for the HCF by building, so pair it with learner-constructed factorisations.
The array/rectangle model is planar; representing it in three dimensions can misleadingly suggest volume, so keep it two-dimensional.
Selecting the fully factorised option or answering yes/no about completeness checks recognition; require learners to produce the factorisation and expand it back to evidence independent construction.
Distinguish factorising (produces a product) from simplifying/collecting like terms (produces fewer terms).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit arithmetic check (all confirmed): HCF(12,8)=4, 12x÷4=3x, 8÷4=2, so 12x+8=4(3x+2); the smaller-factor trap 2(6x+4) is a genuine but incomplete factorisation. HCF(6,9)=3, 6x÷3=2x, 9÷3=3, so 6x+9=3(2x+3). x²+3x=x(x+3). 3(2x+9) wrongly expands to 6x+27, confirming it as an error. All consistent with source fields.

The source frames the reverse area model and the quiz as the strongest fits; these are catalog preferences, not evidence of comparative efficacy or necessity, and have been presented as options with stated affordances/limits rather than universal laws.

The original pedagogy summary's 'widest rectangle' phrasing is ambiguous because a smaller factor actually leaves a longer strip; it has been reworded to 'largest common side / most compact block' so the summary matches the activity descriptions and the intended insight.

Removed the KS3 curriculum claim from the reverse area-model activity's sourceClaims because it supports the topic/objective generally rather than that activity's specific rationale; retained the claims that directly support the inverse-of-expanding and area-representation principles.

probeDeeper: Is 2(6x+4) fully factorised? How can you tell? (counterexample — the incomplete factorisation; the tell is a factor still shared inside the bracket)
Expand your answer back out — do you get 12x+8?
How is factorising related to expanding — what is it 'undoing'?
Now try x² + 3x — is there a common factor that isn't a number?

errorPatterns.pattern: Takes a common factor that is not the highest — 12x+8 → 2(6x+4) — stopping before it is fully factorised.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'is there still a number that divides everything inside the bracket?'; find the HCF of the coefficients first (prime factors), then factorise in one step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The bracket still contains terms with a common factor (6x+4 both divide by 2); the pulled-out number is smaller than the HCF.

errorPatterns.pattern: Drops or fails to divide a term — 6x+9 → 3(2x) losing the 9, or 3(2x+9) with the 9 not divided.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach via the inverse: EVERY original term must be the factor times its bracket entry; divide each term and check by expanding the answer back to 6x+9.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: A term is missing from the bracket, or a term inside was not divided by the factor; expanding back does not give the original.

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives a factorisation but never checks, so an error stands — does not expand the product back to test it.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold the expand-back habit (don't reteach factorising): 'multiply your answer out — do you get what you started with?' Make the check a routine final step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Presents an answer that does not expand to 12x+8 with no attempt to verify; the method is known but the check is skipped.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot find a common factor, or factors only one term / drops a term; the result does not expand back to the original.
responseLevels.full: Extracts the HCF so the bracket has no remaining common factor, divides every term correctly, verifies by expanding back, articulates factorising as the inverse of expanding, and transfers to a common variable factor (x²+3x = x(x+3)).
responseLevels.partial: Extracts A common factor and forms a correct bracket, but not the HIGHEST (leaves a shared factor inside), or omits the expand-back check — factorises but not fully or not reliably.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child this card and say 'factorise this fully, showing your working': 12x + 8. Say nothing about method. Watch whether they pull out the HIGHEST common factor (4) or a smaller one (2), and whether every term inside the bracket is correct.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: 12x+8 has HCF 4 but is ALSO divisible by 2, so a child with partial mastery produces 2(6x+4) — genuinely a factorisation, but not full, because the bracket still shares a factor of 2. Watching which factor they pull out separates full from partial mastery, and asking them to expand back exposes any dropped or mis-divided term.
